items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (via Goldman Sachs — Ben Snider, Ryan Hammond)
items.title: Hedge funds cut AI leverage, but the 0.9 correlation didn't budge
items.idea: 991 hedge funds, $5.4T gross equity exposure ($3.4T long / $2.0T short). The VIP basket had its worst relative month in 20+ years and gross leverage saw one of the decade's sharpest cuts, yet long/short funds are still up ~10% YTD. Correlation between Goldman's VIP basket and its AI basket remains 0.9 — diversification is happening around AI, not away from it. Nasdaq-100 futures shorts are near record and single-stock short interest is unusually high.
items.angle: Near-record NQ shorts plus a still-0.9-correlated long book means a strong NVDA print (Aug 26) could trigger long re-leveraging AND a short squeeze at the same time.
items.tweetA: Hedge funds just had their worst VIP-basket month in 20 years and "de-risked" from AI. Yet the correlation between that basket and the AI basket is still 0.9. They didn't de-risk from AI, they just changed which stocks represent it. Nasdaq shorts near record. NVDA earnings Aug 26 into this setup = fireworks either way. $QQQ $NVDA
items.tweetB: The overlooked structural read in the Goldman hedge fund note: they're not fighting AI anymore, they're fighting EACH OTHER inside it. $3.4T long, $2.0T short, both concentrated in the same names. That's not diversification, that's a crowded room with two doors.

items.title: Beijing reaches for the fiscal lever — but skips the property cannon
items.idea: Q2 China growth slipped to 4.3%, below the 4.5-5% target; July industrial production, consumption and investment all missed. Instead of the old property/infrastructure stimulus, Beijing has funneled interest subsidies and loan guarantees into more than 20 trillion yuan of new lending in the first seven months. Over 2 trillion yuan of bond issuance remains unspent for the rest of the year — August/September is the window to watch for whether it actually deploys.
items.angle: Beijing is deliberately avoiding the property-stimulus playbook this cycle — a policy-relief trade for Chinese equities, but a much weaker signal for the old commodity-supercycle-via-construction thesis.
items.tweetA: China is stimulating without the property cannon this time — 20 trillion yuan in subsidized lending vs. the old infrastructure-and-land playbook. Good setup for a Chinese-equities policy-relief trade. Bad news if you're positioned for a commodity supercycle off Chinese construction like it's 2016. $FXI
items.tweetB: Beijing has 2 trillion yuan of bond issuance still unspent for 2026 and everyone's asking "will they stimulate." Wrong question. The question is whether the money actually lands before Q4 — fiscal spending has been unusually slow to deploy all year. Watch disbursement data, not headlines.

items.title: Nvidia and AMD are now bigger open-source AI publishers than Google or Meta
items.idea: Hugging Face's biannual census: 85.6% of the hub's 2.96M model repos have under 200 lifetime downloads; 1.5% of repos account for 99.2% of all downloads. China's largest monthly open model ran 754B-2.78T params in 2026 vs. the US staying under 130B params in 5 of 7 months. AMD and Nvidia each released 200+ new model repos this year — more than Google or Meta. Only 1 of the top-25-by-downloads repos also appears in the top-25-by-likes.
items.angle: The 'US vs China AI race' framing breaks down when American chipmakers publish open weights specifically to sell silicon — the real trade is chips-as-distribution, not model sovereignty, and it's a trend that builds over months, not a single headline.
items.tweetA: Nvidia and AMD are now bigger open-source AI publishers than Google or Meta. Not because they care about open science — a free model that runs great on your chip is the best sales demo you can ship. Open source AI didn't move to the labs, it moved to the fabs. $NVDA $AMD
items.tweetB: 1.5% of Hugging Face's 2.96M model repos account for 99.2% of downloads. If you're building an AI-model-count-as-innovation-proxy narrative for any country, throw it out — it's a hits business more concentrated than venture returns. Distribution is the entire game, not parameter count.

charts.desc: Report described as built around five charts (download concentration, parameter ceilings by country, publisher rankings, downloads-vs-likes overlap). Charts inside — worth opening.

items.title: Bessent's buyback intervention lasted less than 24 hours
items.idea: Treasury doubled long-end buybacks; Bessent says the program could exceed the $4B already planned, calls it a 'big toolkit,' and says current yields don't reflect fundamentals. The first intervention barely lasted a day before the 10-year was back near 4.70% and the 30-year near 5.25%. Two catalysts now sit on top of this: NVDA earnings Aug 26, then Jackson Hole Aug 27-29.
items.angle: This reads like early-innings yield-curve-control-by-stealth — the market is front-running 'buybacks become QE' psychology even as Bessent insists it isn't; the dollar is absorbing the pressure instead.
items.tweetA: Bessent's buyback intervention lasted less than 24 hours before the 10-year was back at 4.70% and the 30-year at 5.25%. He says it's not QE. The market is already pricing it like the first step toward it. Watch the dollar, not the yield — that's where the pressure is migrating now.
items.tweetB: Two dates now sitting on top of a fragile bond market: NVDA earnings Aug 26, Jackson Hole Aug 27-29. A soft NVDA print AND a hawkish JH would hit a market already leaning on Treasury to backstop the long end. That's a two-strike setup, not a one-shot risk.

items.title: Fund managers turn bullish on China while the data keeps getting worse
items.idea: China sentiment is improving even as activity data deteriorates. China is increasingly framed as a genuine AI-cycle beneficiary rather than a cheap laggard. Net underweights are narrowing but positioning is improving only at the margin — external demand is still doing the heavy lifting while domestic activity lags.
items.angle: Combine with the fiscal-lever item above: sentiment and fundamentals have now diverged on China twice over — this is a bet that Beijing delivers before the divergence snaps back.
items.tweetA: Fund managers are turning bullish on China while the activity data keeps getting worse. That's not a contrarian call, that's a bet Beijing delivers before the divergence closes the other way. If the stimulus lands late, this unwinds fast.
items.tweetB: China is being re-rated as an AI beneficiary, not a cheap catch-up trade. That's worth more than a valuation multiple — it changes who the marginal buyer is. Watch whether that story survives a weak Q3 print without a policy response.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (via Goldman Sachs — Megan Peters)
items.title: US consumer isn't breaking — its second derivative is
items.idea: Goldman's G10 Consumer Dashboard: household balance sheets remain healthy, but sentiment, real income and spending momentum are weakening. Three-month annualized real core retail sales growth has slowed to 1.1%; Goldman expects only 1-1.5% real consumer spending growth in H2 as temporary tax-refund support fades. This is framed as a margin-for-error signal, not a recession call.
items.angle: Earnings estimates still assume resilience while the growth rate of growth fades — that gap is exactly where multiple compression happens, independent of an actual contraction.
items.tweetA: US real core retail sales growth just slowed to 1.1% annualized. Not a crash — a deceleration. But stocks don't need a recession to reprice, they just need earnings estimates built on "resilience" to meet a consumer whose second derivative is already rolling over. That gap is the whole Q4 risk.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching for the US consumer to break. Wrong signal. Watch the RATE of improvement. Balance sheets are fine, spending is fine — but the acceleration that justified this year's multiple is fading, and multiples move on acceleration, not levels.

items.title: BofA's cash level is 'uber-low' — there's no dry powder left to buy the dip
items.idea: BofA's Aug 7-13 Fund Manager Survey (180 managers, $525B AUM): net 56% overweight equities, the highest since November 2021; cash allocations at an 'uber-low' 3.5%. The survey closed the same day the S&P hit its last record high. Crowded-trade reading for long semis fell from 82% to 53% month-over-month, yet 71% still expect no AI capex cuts this year even as AI-bubble risk and hyperscaler capex are the top-named tail risks.
items.angle: The survey is a photograph of peak optimism taken right at the top — before yields, oil and inflation resurfaced — so its real value now is as a positioning map showing how little cash is left to cushion a drawdown.
items.tweetA: BofA's FMS: cash at 3.5%, an "uber-low" in the bank's own words. Net 56% overweight equities, highest since Nov 2021. Survey closed on the exact day the S&P hit its last record high. This isn't a bull signal, it's a photograph of the top of the tank — there's no dry powder left to buy the next dip.
items.tweetB: 71% of fund managers say no AI capex cuts this year. The same survey says AI bubble and hyperscaler capex are the two biggest risks they can name. They're holding the trade they think is the danger. That's not conviction, that's inertia.

items.title: Gold held its gain even after the buyback rate-rally fully reversed
items.idea: Gold ~$4,515/oz, up more than 3% on the week and roughly 11% this month — a third straight weekly gain — despite sitting ~15% below levels seen before the US-Iran conflict escalated in February. The initial yield drop from Treasury's buyback expansion has already been largely retraced, yet gold hasn't given back its move. Bessent has signaled a broader fiscal initiative on borrowing costs is coming.
items.angle: Gold decoupling from the (reversed) rate move is the tell — it's pricing the SIGNAL that Washington won't let long yields clear naturally, i.e. currency-debasement risk, not the usual real-yield correlation.
items.tweetA: Gold held its gain even after the Treasury-buyback rate rally fully reversed. That's the tell: gold isn't trading real yields right now, it's trading the signal that Washington won't let long yields clear naturally. Once bullion decouples from rates like that, it's pricing currency risk, not duration risk. $GLD
items.tweetB: Up 11% this month, still 15% below pre-Iran-conflict highs. Gold's move isn't a geopolitical premium unwinding, it's a NEW premium building — fiscal-dominance risk. Different trade, same asset. Size accordingly.

charts.desc: Gold price action chart likely embedded showing the multi-week rally and the decoupling from the reversed yield move.

items.title: The dollar is becoming America's fiscal release valve
items.idea: Treasury's expanded buybacks aren't large enough to overwhelm a multi-trillion-dollar market, but markets trade the signal before the size. The 30-year pushed toward 5.34% before intervention; Treasury stepped in, yields fell, the dollar weakened, gold surged — all in sequence. Framework: for years higher yields supported the dollar (compensation for risk); now if Washington caps that compensation, the adjustment migrates into the currency instead.
items.angle: This is the cleanest articulation yet of the 'yields capped → dollar is the shock absorber' mechanism — pair with the gold item above as two sides of the same fiscal-dominance trade.
items.tweetA: New reaction function just dropped: for years, higher yields meant a stronger dollar (compensation for risk). Now Washington is capping the long end, so foreign investors get compensated through a weaker dollar instead. Same fiscal risk, different pressure valve. Rethink every dollar rally from here as "how long until Treasury caps this again."
items.tweetB: The 30-year hit 5.34%, Treasury stepped in, yields fell, the dollar fell, gold ripped — all in one sequence. That's not four separate stories, that's one mechanism: fiscal dominance finding its cheapest release valve. Gold and DXY are now trading the same variable from opposite sides.
